**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - SECTION C: PRESCRIBED TEXTS (20 Marks)**

Answer ONE question only.

**1.** Read the following passage from John Ngong Kum's *Walls of Agony* and answer the questions below.

''Better Than Flight''

Years of misery, years of menace
From the ***hardened hands of evil*** thick
As charcoal in darkness dark as night.
Miserable soul conceived in grief,
Born into distress and chaos,  [5]
Raised in poverty and sly affection little or
Yet nursing hope someday to overcome.

I crawled into the wilderness
There to learn how to overcome
A world ***flourishing in bad blood***.  [10]
In tears ***I laboured*** day by day
Shouldering the slashes of the wind
And the corrosive strokes of the sand
To give my existence a human face.

I have come back home  [15]
Yet death ***stalks me still***.
A strange hunger consumes me
As I walk towards my home.
All I need dear Kezeh is wisdom,
A brush and paint for reconstruction.  [20]
The venture will be tough, very tough.
But to challenge corruption to combat
And batter the heart of exploitation
For everyone's good is better than flight.

questions.enonce_markdown: **a)** Briefly say what you consider to be the message in the passage. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answer (66 words)**

The speaker, who grew up in misery and survived years of hardship in the wilderness, has come home to find that death and corruption still threaten him. Even so, he decides not to run away again. With wisdom and the means of rebuilding, symbolised by a brush and paint, he will challenge corruption and exploitation, because working for the good of everyone is better than fleeing.

**Marking**: 2 marks for the central idea (staying to fight corruption and exploitation is better than fleeing), 2 marks for support from the poem (hardship, return home, wisdom, brush and paint, the good of everyone) and clear expression.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**b)** Give the meaning in context of the following expressions:

i. '... *hardened hands of evil*.' (L.2)

ii. '*flourishing in bad blood* (L.9)

iii. '*I laboured* ... ' (L.10)

iv. '*stalks me* ... ' (L.15)

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Meanings in context (1 mark each)**

| Expression | Meaning in context |
|---|---|
| i. *hardened hands of evil* | The cruel, merciless forces or people of wickedness, made callous (like hardened skin) by long practice of oppression. |
| ii. *flourishing in bad blood* | Thriving and growing strong among hatred, hostility and ill feeling: the world the speaker leaves home to understand is one where enmity and evil prosper. |
| iii. *I laboured* | I worked very hard and painfully, I toiled, in tears and day after day, to survive and to build a decent life. |
| iv. *stalks me* | Follows me stealthily and persistently, like a hunter, so that death keeps threatening the speaker. |
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: **c)** Pick out any two devices from the passage and comment on how it has been effectively used. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Answer (2 marks for each device: 1 for the name and example, 1 for the comment on the effect)**

| Device | Example | Comment on its effect |
|---|---|---|
| Simile | 'From the hardened hands of evil thick / As charcoal in darkness dark as night' (L.2-3) | Evil is compared to thick charcoal in the darkness of night: the picture of blackness and density shows how heavy, total and suffocating the speaker's suffering is. |
| Personification | 'Yet death stalks me still' (L.16) | Death is given the movement of a hunter following its prey: the danger is constant, stealthy and personal, so the reader feels the speaker's fear even after his return home. |

Other devices that may be chosen (1 mark for naming, 1 mark for a relevant comment): alliteration and repetition in 'Years of misery, years of menace' and 'hardened hands' (the repeated sounds stress the length and harshness of the suffering); metaphor in 'A world flourishing in bad blood' and 'the heart of exploitation' (evil as something living that grows and can be struck); repetition in 'tough, very tough' (the difficulty of the task).
themes: A Level English - figures of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: **d)** Pick out four verbs in the last stanza and transform them into the past perfect tense. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Answer (1 mark for each verb correctly chosen and transformed)**

The last stanza is the third one ('I have come back home' to 'better than flight').

| Verb in the last stanza (present or present perfect) | Past perfect |
|---|---|
| I **have come** back home | I **had come** back home |
| death **stalks** me still | death **had stalked** me still |
| A strange hunger **consumes** me | A strange hunger **had consumed** me |
| As I **walk** towards my home | As I **had walked** towards my home |

Other verbs that may be chosen: *need* (had needed), *is* (had been), *challenge* (had challenged), *batter* (had battered). The past perfect is formed with *had* + the past participle.

questions.enonce_markdown: **e)** The speaker talks about corruption in the passage. How is this idea of corruption handled in any other two prescribed texts? (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method answer: the prescribed texts are not available here, so no detail of any work is given. Apply this method to two other texts you have studied.**

**What the passage says about corruption**: it is something to be 'challenged' and 'combated'; it is linked with exploitation ('the heart of exploitation'); the speaker is ready to fight it for 'everyone's good'.

**Plan (about 2 marks per text)**

1. Name the first text and its writer. Say who is corrupt (a leader, an institution, a community or a character), in what way (bribery, abuse of power, theft, exploitation of the poor) and how the writer treats it (condemns, ridicules, shows its victims, shows resistance or its end).
2. Do the same with the second text, choosing a different treatment (for example satire in one, tragedy or resistance in the other).
3. One closing sentence comparing the two with the passage.

**Common mistakes**: describing the plot instead of the treatment of corruption; using only one text; naming a text but giving no precise evidence.
